content:
At the end of a debate on the Islamic Dilemma, a member of the audience put a question to the Muslim speaker. By the seventh century, he said, Christians had been copying the scriptures for hundreds of years, in many countries and languages, in churches that did not agree with one another. No one controlled all the copies. So who changed them, when, and how did anyone change every copy at once?

It is a fair question, and it rests on one assumption: that the change, if there was one, came late and had to travel through thousands of manuscripts. The eight answers below test that assumption. They stay on when and how. The site has separate articles on what Islam teaches about taḥrīf, on the charges of alteration made before Islam and on how the Bible and the Quran were copied.

The "every copy" objection pictures a finished Bible, spread across the Roman world, and a forger trying to reach every copy of it. Put that way, the task is impossible, and the objection wins.

The Quran speaks of people "who write the scripture with their own hands, then say, 'This is from Allah'" (Quran 2:79), and of a party "who alter the Scripture with their tongues" (Quran 3:78).[1] The first verse is about writing and attribution, which happen when a book is made. The second is about reading and explaining, which need no copy changed at all.

The Muslim speaker gave the same answer in the debate: on the historians' own account, the problem begins "from the jump", at authorship, before any question of later copying arises. The entries that follow set out what the historians actually say.

None of the four Gospels says who wrote it. Luke opens by saying that "many have undertaken to compile a narrative" and that "it seemed good to me also" to write one for Theophilus (Luke 1:1–3, ESV), but the writer never gives his name.[2] The Fourth Gospel ends with a plural voice vouching for the disciple who wrote it: "we know that his testimony is true" (John 21:24, ESV).

The names come from outside the books. Papias, early in the second century, is reported by Eusebius as saying that Mark wrote down what Peter remembered and that Matthew put sayings together in Hebrew.[3] Irenaeus, around 180, is the first writer who names all four and argues that there can be four Gospels and no more.[4] The oldest papyri that keep a heading, from about 200, carry the titles "according to John" and "according to Luke".[5]

Most critical scholars today hold that the four were written between about 70 and 100, by authors who did not sign them, and that the names were attached later. Conservative scholars defend the traditional names. Either way, the attribution is a matter of second-century tradition, and that is exactly where a change at the source would sit.[6]

Thirteen letters in the New Testament name Paul as their author. Most critical scholars accept seven: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. The other six are disputed, and the three Pastoral Letters are widely held to have been written after his death.[7]

This is the point the Muslim speaker made in answer to the audience question. A letter written in Paul's name by someone else was "changed" at the moment it was written, and every copy made afterwards carried that change faithfully. The copies needed no chasing. The evidence is set out in the site's article on who wrote the letters of Paul, and the case of 2 Peter runs the same way.

Most scholars hold that Mark is the earliest Gospel and that Matthew and Luke both used it as a source. Where they follow Mark, their changes show what an author could do to a text he received.[8]

In Mark, a man calls Jesus "Good Teacher", and Jesus answers: "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18, ESV). In Matthew the same exchange reads: "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good" (Matthew 19:17, ESV).[9] The question that set Jesus apart from God has become a question about the good.

The author of Matthew made this change while composing his Gospel, and every copy of Matthew carries it. That is one answer to "how": the editing happened inside the books, at the start.

Two passages printed in most Bibles are missing from the oldest manuscripts. The first is the ending of Mark after 16:8, where the two great fourth-century codices stop with the women who "said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8, ESV). The second is the woman taken in adultery, John 7:53–8:11.[10]

The story of the adulteress is absent from the two oldest papyri of John, P66 and P75, both of about 200, and from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. Later manuscripts place it in different spots: after John 7:52, after 7:36, at the end of John, or after Luke 21:38. A passage that moves around like that was added from outside the book. The ESV prints it in brackets under a note that the earliest manuscripts do not include it.[11]

Both passages were in circulation before the fourth century, when the copies were fewer and the communities that made them were small. A text grows most easily at that stage, and once a passage sits in the exemplars that later scribes copied, it spreads by ordinary copying. The site's article on 1 John 5:7 traces a later case, a clause that came in through Latin and reached the printed Greek in 1522.

Copyists who knew one Gospel well tended to bring the others into line with it. Textual critics call this harmonisation, and it is one of the commonest kinds of change in the manuscripts.[12]

The Lord's Prayer is the classic case. The ESV, following the oldest manuscripts, gives Luke's short form: "Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come" (Luke 11:2, ESV). The King James Version, following later manuscripts, gives: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth" (Luke 11:2, KJV).[13] The extra words are Matthew's (Matthew 6:9–10). Scribes copied them into Luke because they prayed the prayer in Matthew's form.

All this change needed was a scribe who knew the familiar wording, and a church that copied from his work. Bart Ehrman has argued that some changes of the second and third centuries went further and were made for doctrinal reasons, in the debates over who Jesus was.[14]

The audience question said that the churches were divided and could not have coordinated a change. That is true, and it cuts both ways. They never agreed on which books made up the New Testament either.

The first list that matches the 27 books of the Western canon exactly is the Easter letter of Athanasius of Alexandria in 367, more than three centuries after Jesus.[15] The Syriac Peshitta, the Bible of the Church of the East, has 22 books and leaves out 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church has a larger canon still.[16]

So the question "how could divided churches all change the same text" has a mirror image: divided churches ended up with different scriptures. What a community copied depended on what it had received and what its bishops accepted, and that was settled slowly, place by place.

The classical Muslim answer never required the forgery of every copy. Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) wrote that most Muslims held that some of the wording of the earlier books had been changed, "as much of their meaning has been changed", and that some Muslims held that the change was in meaning only. On either view, he said, the books in their hands do not state the Trinity or the union of God with a man, "neither explicitly nor apparently".[17]

Ibn Ḥazm (d. 1064) made a point that answers the audience question directly. All the Christian churches of his day, he wrote, naming the Melkites, Nestorians, Jacobites and Maronites among them, agree that the Gospels are four histories written by four men at different times. None of them claims that God sent the Gospels down to Jesus.[18] So the divided churches did agree on one thing: the books were human compositions.

That is the Faruqian line too. Al-Fārūqī located Islam's critique of Judaism and Christianity in their historical form, in the texts they came to accept as scripture.[19] The revelations their prophets received from God are, for him, the common ground. A reader can respect the Christian who reveres these books and still ask who wrote them. The fuller survey of classical views is in the site's article on what Islam teaches about corruption.

The bottom line

The change never had to reach every copy. The Gospels were written by unnamed authors and named later, six letters went out under Paul's name that most critical scholars think he did not write, Matthew reworded Mark as he composed, and passages entered the text while the copies were few. Ordinary copying did the rest. The process needed no conspiracy, only time and the work of many human hands.

The question the debate audience asked has a direct answer: the change came early, at the hands of authors, editors and the first copyists, and the churches inherited it. How that bears on the Islamic Dilemma is argued in the site's article on it.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:79 and 3:78, Arabic text from the Ḥafṣ reading (text_qpc_hafs) and English from Saheeh International, both read on api.quran.com.
  2. Luke 1:1–3, English Standard Version.
  3. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.15–16, quoting Papias.
  4. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1 and 3.11.8.
  5. Papyrus 66 (Bodmer II) and Papyrus 75 (Bodmer XIV–XV), both dated to about 200.
  6. Raymond E. Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament (New York: Doubleday, 1997), chapters on each Gospel; Bart D. Ehrman, Forged: Writing in the Name of God (New York: HarperOne, 2011).
  7. Brown, Introduction, chs. 18 to 31; Ehrman, Forged, ch. 3.
  8. Brown, Introduction, ch. 6, on the synoptic problem and the priority of Mark.
  9. Mark 10:17–18 and Matthew 19:16–17, English Standard Version.
  10. Mark 16:8, English Standard Version; Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd ed. (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994), on Mark 16:9–20.
  11. Metzger, Textual Commentary, on John 7:53–8:11; John 7:53–8:11, English Standard Version, with its bracketed note.
  12. Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament, 4th ed. (New York: Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7, on the kinds of change scribes made.
  13. Luke 11:2, English Standard Version and King James Version (1611); Matthew 6:9–10; Metzger, Textual Commentary, on Luke 11:2–4.
  14. Bart D. Ehrman, The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture (New York: Oxford University Press, 1993).
  15. Athanasius, Festal Letter 39 (367).
  16. Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987), on the Syriac and Ethiopian canons.
  17. Ibn Taymiyya, al-Jawāb al-Ṣaḥīḥ li-man Baddala Dīn al-Masīḥ, vol. 2, p. 407, chapter on the alteration of the wording of the Torah and the Gospel (Shamela text, shamela.ws/book/170/791).
  18. Ibn Ḥazm, al-Faṣl fī al-Milal wa al-Ahwāʾ wa al-Niḥal (Cairo: al-Khanji), vol. 2, p. 2 (Shamela text, shamela.ws/book/6521/159).
  19. Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd ed. (Herndon, Va.: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), ch. 2, section II.
